references.text: "The whole earth had one language and the same words." This is the direct background for God's observation in v.6: "they are one people and have all one language".
The human plan to build a city and a tower and make a name for themselves is the concrete project God observes in v.6 as "the beginning of what they do," and that nothing will stop them.
God's direct response to the observation in v.6: He comes down, confuses their language, and scatters them over the whole earth, so that they are no longer "one people with one language".
God's command to Noah and his sons to be fruitful and fill the earth. The unity of humanity at Babel and their desire to stay together stood in opposition to this command.

"I know that you can do all things; no plan is impossible for you." A thematic parallel to the expression in 11:6 that nothing will be impossible for them—but here with reference to God's omnipotence.

On Pentecost, believers spoke in other languages so that everyone heard the gospel in their own language. This can be seen as a gracious reversal of the confusion of languages at Babel, where God uses diversity of languages to unite people instead of dividing them.
Contrast in the use of "one voice": In Exodus it leads to obedience; in Babel, to self-reliance and rebellion.
Theological contrast: Human arrogance at Babel ("nothing impossible") versus God's unstoppable work in Acts.
Theological contrast: Babel's unity based on human power leads to scattering, while Zechariah's prophecy of the gathering of nations in faith in God leads to restoration.
Theological contrast: Babel's "one voice" led to scattering, while Ezekiel's prophecy of "one voice" (one people) leads to restoration under God's leadership.
Direct parallel in the expression "Let us build": In Babel it leads to judgment; in Nehemiah, to restoration under God's leadership.
